newsitem.title: INDIA: India UF, Congress back first low-caste president.
newsitem.headline: India UF, Congress back first low-caste president.

text.p: India's ruling United Front alliance and its main ally the Congress Party on Monday threw their weight behind Vice President Kocheril Raman Narayanan to be elected as the nation's first low-caste president.

The decision-making Steering Committee of the United Front decided to support Narayanan, a journalist-turned diplomat and a former Congress minister, as a candidate for the election of the nation's 11th president.
The Congress party also supported the candidacy of Narayanan for the ceremonial presidential post, Chandrababu Naidu convenor of the United Front, told reporters.
"I met personally Congress president Sitaram Kesri and he said that they (Congress) have decided to support Narayanan," Naidu said.

The decision of both the United Front and Congress to back Narayanan all but paved the way for him to become the next president of the world's most populous democracy, which will mark its 50th year of independence from Britain on August 15.
Presidential elections are scheduled for July 14.
The post is currently held by Shankar Dayal Sharma, a high-caste Hindu Brahmin and a former Congressman.
Since India became a republic in 1950, the presidency has been held by upper-caste Hindus, a Sikh and two Moslems.
Elected members of the federal parliament and state legislatures, which constitute the electoral college, vote for the president's post in India once every five years.
Under the Indian parliamentary system, the president is the titular head of state and has few real powers compared to the prime minister, who is the head of government.
The Indian constitution grants the president the choice of appointing the country's prime minister.
The president also has the final say in proceedings to impeach Supreme Court judges and in appointing state governors.

Earlier, anyone could contest the post of president but Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujaral's cabinet earlier this month approved an ordinance to prevent "frivolous" candidacies for posts of president and vice president.

The measure stipulates that at least 100 members of the electoral college must support a presidential candidate, who must pay a 25,000-rupee ($698) security deposit to file a nomination. The deposit earlier used to be 15,000 rupees.
Traditionally, the vice president is elevated to the presidency, but Narayanan has not announced his candidacy. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
